k-11.4-quantitative-tools.title: 11.4 Perform Quantitative Risk Analysis (continued): probability distributions, Monte Carlo, criticality, sensitivity/tornado, decision trees and EMV, influence diagrams, outputs
k-11.4-quantitative-tools.notes: Interviews generate model inputs (trust, confidentiality); facilitated risk workshops build understanding, consensus, focus and handle conflict and bias. Representations of uncertainty: uncertain durations, costs or resource requirements are modelled as probability distributions - most commonly triangular, normal, lognormal, beta, uniform or discrete; choose carefully. Individual risks may be covered by distributions or modelled as probabilistic branches (optional activities whose chance of occurring in a run equals the risk's probability; best for risks independent of planned activities); related risks (common cause, logical dependency) are modelled with correlation; other uncertainty may be modelled as branches describing alternative paths. Data analysis: simulation - typically Monte Carlo: cost risk uses cost estimates; schedule risk uses the network diagram and duration estimates; integrated cost-schedule analysis uses both; software iterates the model thousands of times with randomly chosen input values; outputs the range of outcomes (end date, cost at completion) as a histogram or a cumulative probability S-curve. Figure 11-13 example: target $2.2M has a 23% chance of being met; expected value $2.35M; 85% chance of costing $2.45M or less. Criticality analysis (schedule): criticality index = how often an element appears on the critical path across runs, as a percentage; focus responses on elements with highest effect. Sensitivity analysis: which risks or uncertainty sources have the most potential impact; correlates variation in outcomes with variation in model elements; tornado diagram shows correlation coefficients ordered by descending strength (Figure 11-14 example items such as manufacturing reactors, a control system failing an installation test, a piling contractor delivering early). Decision tree analysis: choose among alternatives; branches for decisions and chance events with costs and risks; end points are outcomes; evaluate by expected monetary value (EMV) of each branch and select the optimal path. Figure 11-15 (verified arithmetic): build new plant (invest $120M) - strong demand 60% revenue $200M net $80M, weak demand 40% revenue $90M net -$30M; EMV = 0.60 x 80 + 0.40 x (-30) = 48 - 12 = $36M. Upgrade plant (invest $50M) - strong 60% revenue $120M net $70M, weak 40% revenue $60M net $10M; EMV = 0.60 x 70 + 0.40 x 10 = 42 + 4 = $46M. Decision EMV = $46M (upgrade), also the lower-risk choice avoiding a possible $30M loss. Source note: the figure labels these as 'EMV (before costs)' although investment costs are already netted in the branch values - lessons will present the netted calculation and flag the label. Influence diagrams: entities, outcomes and influences with relationships; uncertain elements as ranges or distributions; evaluated by simulation (e.g., Monte Carlo); outputs like S-curves and tornado diagrams. Outputs (risk report updates): assessment of overall project risk exposure - chances of success (probability of meeting key objectives) and degree of inherent variability remaining (range of outcomes); detailed probabilistic analysis (S-curves, tornado diagrams, criticality analysis with narrative; contingency reserve needed for a specified confidence level; risks with greatest effect on the critical path; major drivers of overall risk); prioritised list of individual risks (from sensitivity analysis); trends in results over time; recommended risk responses (inputs to Plan Risk Responses).

k-11.5-plan-responses.title: 11.5 Plan Risk Responses: response criteria, threat and opportunity strategies, contingent responses, overall-risk strategies, secondary and residual risks
k-11.5-plan-responses.notes: Develop options, select strategies and agree actions for overall exposure and individual risks; key benefit: appropriate ways to address risk; allocates resources and inserts activities into documents and the plan; performed throughout. Responses should be appropriate to the risk's significance, cost-effective, realistic, agreed by all parties, and owned by a responsible person; the nominated risk owner develops plans for every sufficiently important risk; the PM also responds to the level of overall risk. Select the strategy or mix most likely to work; structured decision techniques, or for large/complex projects mathematical optimisation or real options analysis. Develop specific actions incl. primary and backup strategies. Contingency plan (fallback plan) for when the selected strategy is not fully effective or an accepted risk occurs. Secondary risks = risks arising directly from implementing a response. Contingency reserve (time or cost) may be allocated with conditions that trigger its use. Inputs: plan (resource management plan - coordinate response resources; risk management plan - roles and thresholds; cost baseline - contingency fund); documents (lessons learned, project schedule, project team assignments, resource calendars, risk register - priority guides strategy: high-priority risks need proactive responses, low-priority ones may only go on the watch list or get contingency; owners, preliminary responses, root causes, triggers and warning signs, near-term risks; risk report - overall exposure and prioritised risks; stakeholder register - potential response owners). Source note: Figure 11-16 and the text list project team assignments as an input, while the data flow Figure 11-17 lists resource breakdown structure in its place - a source inconsistency; lessons follow the ITTO figure and text. EEFs (stakeholder risk appetite and thresholds); OPAs (templates, historical databases, lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment (threat, opportunity, contingent and overall strategies; specialist technical input); interviews with risk owners; facilitation. Strategies for threats (five): escalate (threat outside project scope or response beyond the PM's authority; managed at program, portfolio or other organisational level; PM notifies the right party, who must accept ownership; escalated to the level matching the affected objectives; not monitored further by the team though may be recorded for information); avoid (eliminate the threat or protect the project from its impact; for high-priority, high-probability, large-impact threats; change the plan or the endangered objective to reduce probability to zero or isolate objectives; e.g., remove the cause, extend the schedule, change strategy, reduce scope; clarify requirements, obtain information, improve communication, acquire expertise); transfer (shift ownership and impact to a third party, usually paying a risk premium; insurance, performance bonds, warranties, guarantees, agreements); mitigate (reduce probability and/or impact; early action more effective; less complex processes, more tests, a more stable seller, prototypes; if probability can't be reduced, target severity drivers - e.g., redundancy); accept (acknowledge without proactive action; for low-priority threats or where nothing else is possible or cost-effective; active acceptance - most commonly a contingency reserve of time, money or resources; passive - periodic review only). Strategies for opportunities (five): escalate (as for threats); exploit (ensure it definitely happens, raising probability to 100% - e.g., assign the most talented resources, new technology); share (transfer ownership to a third party who shares the benefit, often with a premium - partnerships, teams, special-purpose companies, joint ventures; choose the owner best able to capture it); enhance (increase probability and/or impact; act early; focus on causes or on factors driving the size of the benefit - e.g., more resources to finish early); accept (active - contingency to take advantage; passive - periodic review). Contingent response strategies: plans executed only under predefined conditions when there will be enough warning; triggers (e.g., missing intermediate milestones, gaining higher priority with a seller) defined and tracked; called contingency or fallback plans. Strategies for overall project risk: avoid (significantly negative and outside thresholds - e.g., remove high-risk scope; cancellation is the most extreme avoidance, only if the threat is and will remain unacceptable); exploit (significantly positive - add high-benefit scope, or modify thresholds with stakeholder agreement); transfer/share (third party manages: transfer for negative with premium, share for positive - collaborative buyer-seller structures, joint ventures, special-purpose companies, subcontracting key elements); mitigate/enhance (replan, change scope and boundaries, priority, resource allocation, delivery times); accept (continue even outside thresholds; active - overall contingency reserve; passive - periodic review). Data analysis: alternatives analysis; cost-benefit analysis - cost effectiveness = (change in impact level) / (implementation cost), higher ratio = more effective. Decision making: multicriteria decision analysis with criteria such as response cost, likely effectiveness, resource availability, timing (urgency, proximity, dormancy), impact level, effect on related risks, secondary risks; strategies may change later if ineffective. Outputs: change requests; plan updates (schedule, cost, quality, resource, procurement management plans - e.g., make-or-buy or contract type changes; scope, schedule, cost baselines); document updates (assumption log, cost forecasts, lessons learned, project schedule - response activities, project team assignments - qualified people, budget, time and technical resources per action, risk register - agreed strategies, specific actions, trigger conditions/symptoms/warning signs, budget and schedule activities, contingency plans and triggers, fallback plans for when a primary response proves inadequate after the risk occurs, residual risks expected to remain after responses or deliberately accepted, secondary risks; risk report). Data flow: change requests to 4.6.

k-11.6-implement-responses.title: 11.6 Implement Risk Responses: ensuring agreed responses are actually executed
k-11.6-implement-responses.notes: Implement agreed risk response plans; key benefit: responses executed as planned to address overall exposure, minimise threats and maximise opportunities; performed throughout. Common problem: teams identify, analyse and plan responses, document them, then take no action; only if risk owners put in the required effort is risk managed proactively. Inputs: risk management plan (roles for allocating response owners, level of detail, thresholds = acceptable target the responses must achieve); documents (lessons learned, risk register - agreed responses and owners, risk report - overall exposure, agreed strategy, major risks and responses); OPAs (lessons learned repository on response effectiveness). Tools: expert judgment (validate or modify responses, implement efficiently); influencing (owners outside the team or with competing demands may need encouragement to act); PMIS (integrate response activities with schedule, resource and cost software). Outputs: change requests (to cost and schedule baselines or other components); document updates (issue log, lessons learned, project team assignments, risk register - changes to agreed responses, risk report). Data flow: change requests to 4.6.

k-11.7-monitor-risks.title: 11.7 Monitor Risks: what monitoring determines, inputs (part 1)
k-11.7-monitor-risks.notes: Monitor implementation of agreed responses, track identified risks, identify and analyse new risks, evaluate risk process effectiveness; key benefit: decisions based on current information about overall exposure and individual risks; performed throughout. Uses execution performance information to determine whether: responses are effective; overall risk has changed; status of individual risks has changed; new risks have arisen; the risk approach is still appropriate; assumptions are still valid; risk policies and procedures are followed; cost or schedule contingency reserves need modification; project strategy is still valid. Inputs: risk management plan (how and when to review, policies, roles, reporting formats); documents (issue log - updated issues may require risk register updates, lessons learned, risk register - risks, owners, responses, actions, control actions to assess response effectiveness, symptoms and warning signs, residual and secondary risks, watch list; risk report). (Continued on PDF 493.) Data flow: WPD from 4.3; WPR from 4.5; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6.
